entries.378eb2fa1eedebfaad7b222ff265977a0bc38047: <div sID="gen16580" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="48" osisID="Isa.48" sID="Isa.48"/> <div eID="gen16580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16581" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16582" type="x-p"/> God, having in the foregoing chapter reckoned with the Babylonians, and shown them their sins and the desolation that was coming upon them for their sins, to show that he hates sin wherever he finds it and will not connive at it in his own people, comes, in this chapter, to show the house of Jacob their sins, but, withal, the mercy God had in store for them notwithstanding; and he therefore sets their sins in order before them, that by their repentance and reformation they might be prepared for that mercy. I. He charges them with hypocrisy in that which is good and obstinacy in that which is evil, especially in their idolatry, notwithstanding the many convincing proofs God had given them that he is God alone, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1-Isa.47.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. He assures them that their deliverance would be wrought purely for the sake of God's own name and not for any merit of theirs, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.9-Isa.47.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. III. He encourages them to depend purely upon God's power and promise for this deliverance, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. IV. He shows them that, as it was by their own sin that they brought themselves into captivity, so it would be only by the grace of God that they would obtain the necessary preparatives for their enlargement, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.16-Isa.47.19">ver. 16-19</reference>. V. He proclaims their release, yet with a proviso that the wicked shall have no benefit by it, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.20-Isa.47.22">ver. 20-22</reference>.
entries.81322fe75cd92dd0827aa830dd0df99f4c58fe4a: <div eID="gen16582" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16581" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Expostulation with His People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16583" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Hear ye this, O house of Jacob, which are called by the name of Israel, and are come forth out of the waters of Judah, which swear by the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and make mention of the God of Israel, <hi type="italic">but</hi> not in truth, nor in righteousness. <hi type="super">2</hi> For they call themselves of the holy city, and stay themselves upon the God of Israel; The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <hi type="super">3</hi> I have declared the former things from the beginning; and they went forth out of my mouth, and I showed them; I did <hi type="italic">them</hi> suddenly, and they came to pass. <hi type="super">4</hi> Because I knew that thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> obstinate, and thy neck <hi type="italic">is</hi> an iron sinew, and thy brow brass; <hi type="super">5</hi> I have even from the beginning declared <hi type="italic">it</hi> to thee; before it came to pass I showed <hi type="italic">it</hi> thee: lest thou shouldest say, Mine idol hath done them, and my graven image, and my molten image, hath commanded them. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou hast heard, see all this; and will not ye declare <hi type="italic">it?</hi> I have showed thee new things from this time, even hidden things, and thou didst not know them. <hi type="super">7</hi> They are created now, and not from the beginning; even before the day when thou heardest them not; lest thou shouldest say, Behold, I knew them. <hi type="super">8</hi> Yea, thou heardest not; yea, thou knewest not; yea, from that time <hi type="italic">that</hi> thine ear was not opened: for I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously, and wast called a transgressor from the womb. <div eID="gen16583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16584" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, <div eID="gen16584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16585" type="x-p"/> I. The hypocritical profession which many of the Jews made of religion and relation to God. To those who made such a profession the prophet is here ordered to address himself, for their conviction and humiliation, that they might own God's justice in what he had brought upon them. Now observe here, <div eID="gen16585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16586" type="x-p"/> 1. How high their profession of religion soared, what a fair show they made in the flesh and how far they went towards heaven, what a good livery they wore and what a good face they put upon a very bad heart. (1.) They were the <hi type="italic">house of Jacob;</hi> they had a place and a name in the visible church. <hi type="italic">Jacob have I loved.</hi> Jacob is God's chosen; and they are not only retainers to his family, but descendants from him. (2.) They were <hi type="italic">called by the name of Israel,</hi> an honourable name; they were of that people to whom pertained both the giving of the law and the promises. <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">a prince with God;</hi> and they prided themselves in being of that princely race. (3.) <hi type="italic">They came forth out of the waters of Judah,</hi> and thence were called <hi type="italic">Jews;</hi> they were of the royal tribe, the tribe of which Shiloh was to come, the tribe that adhered to God when the rest revolted. (4.) They <hi type="italic">swore by the name of the Lord,</hi> and thereby owned him to be the true God, and their God, and gave glory to him as the righteous Judge of all. They <hi type="italic">swore to the name of the Lord</hi> (so it may be read); they took an oath of allegiance to him as their King and joined themselves to him in covenant. (5.) They <hi type="italic">made mention of the God of Israel</hi> in their prayers and praises; they often spoke of him, observed his memorials, and pretended to be very mindful of him. (6.) They <hi type="italic">called themselves of the holy city,</hi> and, when they were captives in Babylon, purely from a principle of honour, and jealousy for their native country, they valued themselves upon their interest in it. Many, who are themselves unholy, are proud of their relation to the church, the holy city. (7.) They <hi type="italic">stayed themselves upon the God of Israel,</hi> and boasted of his promises and his covenant with them; they <hi type="italic">leaned on the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mic. iii. 11</reference>. And, if they were asked concerning their God, they could say, "<hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts is his name,</hi> the Lord of all;" happy are we therefore, and very great, who have relation to him! <div eID="gen16586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16587" type="x-p"/> 2. How low their profession of religion sunk, notwithstanding all this. It was all in vain; for it was all a jest; it was <hi type="italic">not in truth and righteousness.</hi> Their hearts were not true nor right in these professions. Note, All our religious professions avail nothing further than they are made in truth and righteousness. If we be not sincere in them, we do but <hi type="italic">take the name of the Lord our God in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen16587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16588" type="x-p"/> II. The means God used, and the method he took, to keep them close to himself, and to prevent their turning aside to idolatry. The many excellent laws he gave them, with their sanctions, and the hedges about them, it seems, would not serve to restrain them from that sin which did most easily beset them, and therefore to those God added remarkable prophecies, and remarkable providences in pursuance of those prophecies, which were all designed to convince them that their God was the only true God and that it was therefore both their duty and interest to adhere to him. 1. He both dignified and favoured them with remarkable prophecies (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have declared the former things from the beginning.</hi> Nothing material happened to their nation from its original which was not prophesied of before—their bondage in Egypt, their deliverance thence, the situation of their tribes in Canaan, &c. All these things <hi type="italic">went forth out of God's mouth and he showed them.</hi> Herein they were honoured above any nation, and even their curiosity was gratified. Their prophecies were such as they could rely upon, and such as concerned themselves and their own nation; and they were all verified by the accomplishment of them. <hi type="italic">I did them suddenly,</hi> when they were least expected by themselves or others, and therefore could not be foreseen by any but a divine prescience. <hi type="italic">I did them and they came to pass;</hi> for what God does he does effectually. The very calamities they were now groaning under in Babylon God did from the beginning declare to them by Moses, as the certain consequences of their apostasy from God, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31 Deut.28.36 Deut.29.28">Lev. xxvi. 31, &c.; Deut. xxviii. 36, &c.; xxix. 28</reference>. He also declared to them their return to God, and to their own land again, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.4 Lev.26.44-Lev.26.45">Deut. xxx. 4, &c.; Lev. xxvi. 44, 45</reference>. Thus he showed them how he would deal with them long before it came to pass. Let them compare their present state together with the deliverance they had now in prospect with what was written in the law, and they would find the scripture exactly fulfilled. 2. He both dignified and favoured them with remarkable providence (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have shown thee new things from this time.</hi> Besides the general view given from the beginning of God's proceedings with them, he showed them new things by the prophets of their own day, and created them. They were <hi type="italic">hidden things,</hi> which they could not otherwise know, as the prophecy concerning Cyrus and the exact time of their release out of Babylon. These things God <hi type="italic">created now,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.7">v. 7</reference>. Their restoration was in effect their creation, and they had a promise of it not from the beginning, but of late; for to prevent their apostasy from God, or to recover them, prophecy was kept up among them. Yet it was told them when they could not come to the knowledge of it in any other way than by divine revelation. "Consider," says God, "how much soever it is talked of now among you and expected, it was told you by the prophets, when it was the furthest thing from your thoughts, when you had not heard it, when you had not known it, nor had any reason to expect it, and when your ear was not opened concerning it (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.7-Isa.48.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), when the thing seemed utterly impossible, and you would scarcely have given any one the hearing who should have told you of it." God had shown them hidden things which were out of the reach of their knowledge, and done for them great things, out of the reach of their power: "Now," says he (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.6">v. 6</reference>), "<hi type="italic">thou hast heard; see all this.</hi> Thou hast heard the prophecy; see the accomplishment of it, and observe whether the word and works of God do not exactly agree; <hi type="italic">and will you not declare it,</hi> that as you have heard so you have seen? Will you not own that the Lord is the true God, the only true God, that he has the knowledge and power which no creature has and which none of the gods of the nations can pretend to? Will you not own that your God has been a good God to you? Declare this to his honour, and your own shame, who have dealt so deceitfully with him and preferred others before him." <div eID="gen16588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16589" type="x-p"/> III. The reasons why God would take this method with them. <div eID="gen16589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16590" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he would anticipate their boastings of themselves and their idols. (1.) God by his prophets told them beforehand of their deliverance, lest they should attribute the accomplishment of it to their idols. Thus he saw it necessary to secure the glory of it to himself, which otherwise would have been given by some of them to their graven images: "I spoke of it," says God, "<hi type="italic">lest thou shouldst say, My idol has done it or has commanded it to be done,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">v. 5</reference>. There were those that would be apt to say so, and so would be confirmed in their idolatry by that which was intended to cure them of it. But they would now be for ever precluded from saying this; for, if the idols had done it, the prophets of the idols would have foretold it; but, the prophets of the Lord having foretold it, it was no doubt the power of the Lord that effected it. (2.) God foretold it by his prophets, lest they should assume the foresight of it to themselves. Those that were not so profane as to have ascribed the thing itself to an idol were yet so proud as to have pretended that by their own sagacity they foresaw it, if God had not been beforehand with them and spoken first: <hi type="italic">Lest thou shouldst say, Behold, I knew them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.7">v. 7</reference>. Thus vain men, who would be thought wise, commonly undervalue a thing which is really great and surprising with this suggestion, that it was no more than they expected and they knew it would come to this. To anticipate this, and that this boasting might for ever be excluded, God told them of it before the day, when as yet they dreamed not of it. God has said and done enough to prevent men's boastings of themselves, and that <hi type="italic">no flesh may glory in his presence,</hi> and, if it have not the intended effect, it will aggravate the sin and ruin of the proud; and, sooner, or later, <hi type="italic">every mouth shall be stopped, and all flesh shall become silent before God.</hi> <div eID="gen16590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16591" type="x-p"/> 2. Because he would leave them inexcusable in their obstinacy. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he took this pains with them, because he knew they were obstinate, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">v. 4</reference>. He knew they were so obstinate and perverse that, if he had not supported the doctrine of providence by prophecy, they would have had the impudence to deny it, and would have said that their idol had done that which God did. He knew very well, (1.) How wilful they would be, and how fully bent they would be upon that which is evil: <hi type="italic">I knew that thou wast hard;</hi> so the word is. There were prophecies as well as precepts which God gave them because of the hardness of their hearts: "<hi type="italic">Thy neck is an iron sinew,</hi> unapt to yield and submit to the yoke of God' commandments, unapt to turn and look back upon his dealings with thee or look up to his displeasure against thee; not flexible to the will of God, nor pliable to his intentions, nor manageable by his word or providence. <hi type="italic">Thy brow is brass;</hi> thou art impudent and canst not blush, insolent and wilt not fear or give back, but wilt thrust on in the way of thy heart." God uses means to bring sinners to comply with him, though he knows they are obstinate. (2.) How deceitful they would be and how insincere in that which is good, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">v. 8</reference>. God sent his prophets to them, but they did not hear, they would not know, and it was no more than was expected, considering what they had been. Thou <hi type="italic">wast called,</hi> and not miscalled, <hi type="italic">a transgressor from the womb.</hi> Ever since they were first formed into a people they were prone to idolatry; they brought with them out of Egypt a strange addictedness to that sin; and they were murmurers as soon as ever they began their march to Canaan. They were justly upbraided with it then, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">Deut. ix. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.24">24</reference>. Therefore <hi type="italic">I knew that thou wouldst deal very treacherously.</hi> God foresaw their apostasy, and gave this reason for it, that he had always found them false and fickle, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">Deut. xxxi. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.29">29</reference>. This is applicable to particular persons. We are all born children of disobedience; we were called <hi type="italic">transgressors from the womb,</hi> and therefore it is easy to foresee that we shall deal treacherously, very treacherously. Where original sin is actual sin will follow of course. God knows it, and yet deals not with us according to our deserts.
entries.d046fb51a3de2ce6cbb1af67c91cc5bac042d459: <div eID="gen16591" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to God's People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16592" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> For my name's sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off. <hi type="super">10</hi> Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction. <hi type="super">11</hi> For mine own sake, <hi type="italic">even</hi> for mine own sake, will I do <hi type="italic">it:</hi> for how should <hi type="italic">my name</hi> be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another. <hi type="super">12</hi> Hearken unto me, O Jacob and Israel, my called; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> he; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the first, I also <hi type="italic">am</hi> the last. <hi type="super">13</hi> Mine hand also hath laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand hath spanned the heavens: <hi type="italic">when</hi> I call unto them, they stand up together. <hi type="super">14</hi> All ye, assemble yourselves, and hear; which among them hath declared these <hi type="italic">things?</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath loved him: he will do his pleasure on Babylon, and his arm <hi type="italic">shall be on</hi> the Chaldeans. <hi type="super">15</hi> I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, have spoken; yea, I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous. <div eID="gen16592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16593" type="x-p"/> The deliverance of God's people out of their captivity in Babylon was a thing upon many accounts so improbable that there was need of line upon line for the encouragement of the faith and hope of God's people concerning it. Two things were discouraging to them—their own unworthiness that God should do it for them and the many difficulties in the thing itself; now, in these verses, both these discouragements are removed, for here is, <div eID="gen16593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16594" type="x-p"/> I. A reason why God would do it for them, though they were unworthy; not for their sake, be it known to them, but <hi type="italic">for his name's sake, for his own sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.9-Isa.48.11">v. 9-11</reference>. 1. It is true they had been very provoking, and God had been justly angry with them. Their captivity was the punishment of their iniquity; and if, when he had them in Babylon, he had left them to pine away and perish there, and made the desolations of their country perpetual, he would only have dealt with them according to their sins, and it was what such a sinful people might expect from an angry God. "But," says God, "<hi type="italic">I will defer my anger</hi>" (or, rather, <hi type="italic">stifle and suppress it</hi>); "I will make it appear that I am slow to wrath, and will refrain from thee, not pour upon thee what I justly might, that I should cut thee off from being a people." And why will God thus stay his hand? <hi type="italic">For my name's sake;</hi> because this people was called by his name, and made profession of his name, and, if they were cut off, the enemies would blaspheme his name. <hi type="italic">It is for my praise;</hi> because it would redound to the honour of his mercy to spare and reprieve them, and, if he continued them to be to him a people, they might be to him for a name and a praise. 1. It is true they were very corrupt and ill-disposed, but God would himself refine them, and make them fit for the mercy he intended for them: "<hi type="italic">I have refined thee,</hi> that thou mightest be made a vessel of honour." Though he does not find them meet for his favour, he will make them so. And this accounts for his bringing them into the trouble, and continuing them in it so long as he did. It was not to cut them off, but to do them good. It was to refine them, <hi type="italic">but not as silver,</hi> or <hi type="italic">with silver,</hi> not so thoroughly as men refine their silver, which they continue in the furnace till all the dross is separated from it; if God should take that course with them, they would be always in the furnace, for they are all dross, and, as such, might justly be put away (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.119">Ps. cxix. 119</reference>) as reprobate silver, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.30">Jer. vi. 30</reference>. He therefore takes them as they are, refined in part only, and not thoroughly. "<hi type="italic">I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction,</hi> that is, I have made thee a choice one by the good which the affliction has done thee, and then designed thee for great things." Many have been brought home to God as chosen vessels and a good work of grace has been begun in them in the furnace of affliction. Affliction is no bar to God's choice, but subservient to his purpose. 3. It is true they could not pretend to merit at God's hand so great a favour as their deliverance out of Babylon, which would put such an honour upon them and bring them so much joy; therefore, says God, <hi type="italic">For my own sake, even for my own sake, will I do it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.11">v. 11</reference>. See how the emphasis is laid upon that; for it is a reason that cannot fail, and therefore the resolution grounded upon it cannot fall to the ground. God will do it, not because he owes them such a favour, but to save the honour of his own name, that that may not be polluted by the insolent triumphs of the heathen, who, in triumphing over Israel, thought they triumphed over the God of Israel and imagined their gods too hard for him. This was plainly the language of Belshazzar's revels, when he profaned the holy vessels of God's temple at the same time that he praised his idols (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.2">Dan. v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">4</reference>), and of the Babylonians' demand (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Ps. cxxxvii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Sing us one of the songs of Zion.</hi> God will <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> deliver his people, because he will not suffer his glory to be thus given to another. Moses pleaded this often with God: Lord, <hi type="italic">what will the Egyptians say?</hi> Note, God is jealous for the honour of his own name, and will not suffer the wrath of man to proceed any further than he will make it turn to his praise. And it is matter of comfort to God's people that, whatever becomes of them, God will secure his own honour; and, as far as is necessary to that, God will work deliverance for them. <div eID="gen16594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16595" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a proof that God could do it for them, though they were unable to help themselves and the thing seemed altogether impracticable. Let Jacob and Israel hearken to this, and believe it, and take the comfort of it. They are God's called, <hi type="italic">called according to his purpose,</hi> called by him out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Hos. xi. 1</reference>) and now out of Babylon, a people whom with a distinguishing favour he calls by name, and to whom he calls. They are his called, for they are called to him, called by his name, and called his; and therefore he will look after them, and they may be assured that, as he will deliver them for his own sake, so he will deliver them by his own strength. They need not fear them, for, 1. He is God alone, and the eternal God (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am he</hi> who can do what I will and will do what is best, he whom none can compare with, much less contend with. <hi type="italic">I am the first; I also am the last.</hi>" Who can be too quick for him that is the first, or anticipate him? Who can be too hard for him that is the last, and will keep the field against all opposers, and will reign till they are all made his footstool? What room then is left to doubt of their deliverance when <hi type="italic">he</hi> undertakes it whose designs cannot but be well laid, for he is the first, and well executed, for he is the last. As for this God, his work is perfect. 2. He is the God that made the world, and he that did that can do any thing, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.13">v. 13</reference>. Look we down? We see the earth firm under us, and feel it so; it was his hand that <hi type="italic">laid the foundation</hi> of it. Look we up? We see the heavens spread out as a canopy over our heads, and it was his hand that spread them, that <hi type="italic">spanned</hi> them, that stretched them out, and did it by an exact measure, as the workman sometimes metes out his work by spans. This intimates that God has a vast reach and can compass designs of the greatest extent. <hi type="italic">If the palm of his right hand</hi> (so the margin reads it) has gone so far as to stretch out the heavens, what will he do with his outstretched arm? Yet this is not all: he has not only made the heavens and the earth, and therefore he in whom our hope and help is omnipotent (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">Ps. cxxiv. 8</reference>), but he has the command of all the hosts of both; when he calls them into his service, to go on his errands, they stand up together, they come at the call, they answer to their names: "Here we are; what wilt thou have us to do?" They stand up, not only in reverence to their Creator, but in a readiness to execute his orders: <hi type="italic">They stand up together,</hi> unanimously concurring, and helping one another in the service of their Maker. If God therefore will deliver his people, he cannot be at a loss for instruments to be employed in effecting their deliverance. 3. He has already foretold it, and, having infinite knowledge, so that he foresaw it, no doubt he has almighty power to effect it: "<hi type="italic">All you</hi> of the house of Jacob, <hi type="italic">assemble yourselves, and hear</hi> this for your comfort, <hi type="italic">Which among them,</hi> among the gods of the heathen, or their wise men, <hi type="italic">has declared these things,</hi> or could declare them?" <reference osisRef="Isa.48.14">v. 14</reference>. They had no foresight of them at all, but those who consulted them were very confident that Babylon should be a lady for ever and Israel perpetual slave; and their oracles did not give them the least hint to the contrary, to undeceive them; whereas God by his prophets had given notice to the Jews, long before, of their captivity and the destruction of Jerusalem, as he had now likewise given them notice of their release (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">I, even I, have spoken;</hi> and he would not have spoken it if he could not have made it good: none could out-see him, and therefore we may be sure that none could outdo him. 4. The person is pitched upon who is to be employed in this service, and the measures are concerted in the divine counsels, which are unalterable. Cyrus is the man who must do it; and it tends much to strengthen our assurance that a thing shall be done when we are particularly informed how and by whom. It is not left at uncertainty who shall do it, but the matter is fixed. (1.) It is one whom God is well pleased in, upon this account, because he is designed for this service: <hi type="italic">The Lord has loved him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.14">v. 14</reference>); he has done him this favour, this honour, to make him an instrument in the redemption of his people and therein a type of the great Redeemer, God's beloved Son, <hi type="italic">in whom he was well pleased.</hi> Those God does a great kindness to, and has a great kindness for, whom he makes serviceable to his church. (2.) It is one to whom God will give authority and commission: <hi type="italic">I have called him,</hi> have given him a sufficient warrant, and therefore will bear him out. (3.) It is one whom God will by a series of providences lead to this service: "<hi type="italic">I have brought him from a far</hi> country, brought him to engage against Babylon, brought him step by step, quite beyond his own intentions." Whom God calls he will bring, will <hi type="italic">cause them to come</hi> (so the word is), to come at the call. (4.) It is one whom God will own and give success to. Cyrus will <hi type="italic">do God's pleasure on Babylon,</hi> that which it is his pleasure should be done and which he will be pleased with the doing of, though Cyrus has ends of his own to serve and has no regard either to the will of God or to his favour in the doing of it. <hi type="italic">His arm</hi> (Cyrus's army, and in it God's arm) <hi type="italic">shall</hi> come, and <hi type="italic">be upon the Chaldeans,</hi> to bring them down (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.14">v. 14</reference>); for, if God call him and bring him, he will certainly <hi type="italic">make his way prosperous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.15">v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we may hope to prosper in our way when we follow a divine call and guidance.
entries.8407570fdd5eae04e152cf341f927f66d605ace7: <div eID="gen16595" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to God's People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Come ye near unto me, hear ye this; I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time that it was, there <hi type="italic">am</hi> I: and now the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , and his Spirit, hath sent me. <hi type="super">17</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God which teacheth thee to profit, which leadeth thee by the way <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou shouldest go. <hi type="super">18</hi> O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea: <hi type="super">19</hi> Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me. <hi type="super">20</hi> Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans, with a voice of singing declare ye, tell this, utter it <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the end of the earth; say ye, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath redeemed his servant Jacob. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they thirsted not <hi type="italic">when</hi> he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out. <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no peace, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , unto the wicked. <div eID="gen16596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16597" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, Jacob and Israel are summoned to hearken to the prophet speaking in God's name, or rather to God speaking in and by the prophet, and that as a type of the great prophet by whom God has in these last days spoken unto us, and that is sufficient: <hi type="italic">Come near</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and hear this.</hi> Note, Those that would hear and understand what God says must come near, and approach to him; let them come as near as they can. Let those that have hearkened to the tempter now come near, and hear this, that they may be confirmed in their resolutions to serve God. Those that draw nigh to God may depend upon this, that his secret shall be with them. Here, <div eID="gen16597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16598" type="x-p"/> I. God refers them to what he hath both said to them and done for them formerly, which if they would reflect upon, they might thence fetch great encouragement to trust in God at this time. 1. He had always spoken plainly to them <hi type="italic">from the beginning,</hi> by Moses and all the prophets: <hi type="italic">I have not spoken in secret,</hi> but publicly, from the top of Mount Sinai, and in the chief places of concourse, the solemn assemblies of their tribes; he did not deliver his oracles obscurely and ambiguously, but so that they might be understood, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.2">Hab. ii. 2</reference>. 2. He had always acted wonderfully for them: "<hi type="italic">From the time</hi> that they were first formed into a people <hi type="italic">there I am,</hi> there have I been resident among them and presiding in their affairs (he sent them prophets, raised them up judges, and frequently appeared for them), and therefore there I will be still." He that has been with his people hitherto will be to the end. <div eID="gen16598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16599" type="x-p"/> II. The prophet himself, as a type of the great prophet, asserts his own commission to deliver this message: <hi type="italic">Now the Lord God</hi> (the same that spoke from the beginning and did not speak in secret) <hi type="italic">has by his Spirit sent me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">v. 16</reference>. The Spirit of God is here spoken of as a person distinct from the Father and the Son, and having a divine authority to send prophets. Note, Whom God sends the Spirit sends. Those whom God commissions for any service the Spirit in some measure qualifies for it; and those may speak boldly, and must be heard obediently, whom God and his Spirit send. As that which the prophet says to the same purport with this (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">ch. lxi. 1</reference>) is applied to Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.21">Luke iv. 21</reference>), so may this be; the Lord God sent him, and he had the Spirit without measure. <div eID="gen16599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16600" type="x-p"/> III. God by the prophet sends them a gracious message for their support and comfort under their affliction. The preface to this message is both awful and encouraging (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus saith Jehovah,</hi> the eternal God, <hi type="italic">thy Redeemer,</hi> that has often been so, that has engaged to be so, and will be faithful to the engagement, for he is <hi type="italic">the Holy One,</hi> that cannot deceive, <hi type="italic">the Holy One of Israel,</hi> that will not deceive them. The same words that introduce the law, and give authority to that, introduce the promise, and give validity to that: "<hi type="italic">I am the Lord thy God,</hi> whom thou mayest depend upon as in relation to thee and in covenant with thee." <div eID="gen16600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16601" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the good work which God undertakes to fulfil in them. He that is their Redeemer, in order to that, will be, (1.) Their instructor: "<hi type="italic">I am thy God that teaches thee to profit,</hi> that is, teaches thee such things as are profitable for thee, things that belong to thy peace." By <hi type="italic">this</hi> God shows himself to be a God in covenant with us, by his <hi type="italic">teaching us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.10-Heb.8.11">Heb. viii. 10, 11</reference>); and none teaches like him, for he gives an understanding. Whom God redeems he teaches; whom he designs to deliver out of their afflictions he first teaches to profit by their afflictions, makes them partakers of his holiness, for that is the <hi type="italic">profit for which he chastens us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">Heb. xii. 10</reference>. (2.) Their guide: <hi type="italic">He leads them</hi> to the way and <hi type="italic">in the way by which they should go.</hi> He not only enlightens their eyes, but directs their steps. By his grace he leads them in the way of duty, by his providence he leads them in the way of deliverance. Happy are those that are under such a guidance! <div eID="gen16601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16602" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the good-will which God declares he had for them by his good wishes concerning them, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.18-Isa.48.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. He had indeed brought them into captivity, but it was owing to themselves, nor did he afflict them willingly. (1.) As when he gave them his law he earnestly wished they might be obedient (<hi type="italic">O that there were such a heart in them!</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.5.29">Deut. v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">O that they were wise!</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">Deut. xxxii. 29</reference>), so, when he had punished them for the breach of his law, he wished they had been obedient: <hi type="italic">O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments!</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">O that my people had hearkened unto me!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.81.13">Ps. lxxxi. 13</reference>. This confirms what God had said and sworn, that he has <hi type="italic">no pleasure in the death of sinners.</hi> (2.) He assures them that, if they had been obedient, that would not only have prevented their captivity, but would have advanced and perpetuated their prosperity. He had abundance of good things ready to bestow upon them if their sins had not <hi type="italic">turned them away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.1-Isa.59.2">ch. lix. 1, 2</reference>. [1.] They should have been carried on in a constant uninterrupted stream of prosperity: "<hi type="italic">Thy peace should have been as a river;</hi> thou shouldst have enjoyed a series of mercies, one continually following another, as the waters of a river, which always last." <hi type="italic">Labitur, et labetur in omne volubilis ævum—It flows, and will for ever flow;</hi> not like the waters of a land-flood, which are soon gone. [2.] Their virtue and honour, and the justice of their cause, should in all cases have borne down opposition by their own strength, <hi type="italic">as the waves of the sea.</hi> Such should their righteousness have been that nothing should have stood before it; whereas, now they had been disobedient, the current of their prosperity was interrupted, and their righteousness overpowered. [3.] The rising generation should have been very numerous and very prosperous; whereas they were now very few, as appears by the small number of the returning captives (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.64">Ezra ii. 64</reference>), not so many as of one tribe when they came out of Egypt. They should have been <hi type="italic">numberless as the sand,</hi> according to the promise (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 17</reference>), which they had forfeited the benefit of: "<hi type="italic">The offspring of thy bowels</hi> would have been innumerable, <hi type="italic">like the gravel of the sea,</hi> if thy righteousness had been irresistible and unconquerable as the waves of the sea." [4.] The honour of Israel should still have been unstained, untouched: <hi type="italic">His name should not have been cut off,</hi> as now it is in the land of Israel, which is either desolate or inhabited by strangers; nor should it have <hi type="italic">been destroyed from before God.</hi> We cannot reckon the name either of a family or of a kingdom destroyed till it is destroyed from before God, till it ceases to be a name in his holy place. Now God tells them thus what he would have done for them if they had persevered in their obedience, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That they might be the more humbled for their sins, by which they had forfeited such rich mercies. Note, <hi type="italic">This</hi> should engage us (I might say, enrage us) against sin, that it has not only deprived us of the good things we have enjoyed, but prevented the good things God had in store for us. It will make the misery of the disobedient the more intolerable to think how happy they might have been. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That his mercy might appear the more illustrious in working deliverance for them, though they had forfeited it and rendered themselves unworthy of it. Nothing but a prerogative of mercy would have saved them. <div eID="gen16602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16603" type="x-p"/> 3. Here is assurance given of the great work which God designed to work for them, even their salvation out of their captivity, when he had accomplished his work in them. <div eID="gen16603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16604" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a commission granted them to leave Babylon. God proclaimed, long before Cyrus did, that whoever would might return to his own land (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">v. 20</reference>): "You have a full discharge sent you: <hi type="italic">Go you forth out of Babylon;</hi> the prison-doors are thrown open, and the trumpet sounds, proclaiming a release." Perhaps with this word, as a means, the Spirit of the Lord stirred up the spirits of those that did take the benefit of Cyrus's proclamation (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezra i. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Flee you from the Chaldeans,</hi> not with an ignominious stolen flight, as Jacob fled from Laban, but with a holy disdain, as scorning to stay any longer among them; flee you, not silently and sorrowfully, but with a voice, with a voice of singing, as they fled of old out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.1">Exod. xv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen16604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16605" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is the news of this sent to all parts: "Let it be declared; let it be told; let it be uttered; make it to be heard by the most remote, by the most remiss; send the tidings of it by word of mouth; send it by writing, from city to city, from kingdom to kingdom, even to the utmost regions, <hi type="italic">to the ends of the earth.</hi>" This was a figure of the publishing of the gospel to all the world; but that brings glad tidings which all the world is concerned in, this only that which it is fit all should take notice of, that they may be invited by it to forsake their idols and come into the service of the God of Israel. Let them all know then, [1.] That those whom God owns for his are such as he has dearly bought and paid for: <hi type="italic">The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob;</hi> he has done it formerly, when he brought them out of Egypt, and now he is about to do it again. Jacob was God's servant, and therefore he redeemed him; for what had other masters to do with God's servants? Israel is God's son, therefore Pharaoh must let him go. God redeemed Jacob, and therefore it was fit that he should be his servant (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Ps. cxvi. 16</reference>); the bonds God had loosed tied them the faster to him. He that redeemed us has an unquestionable right to us. [2.] That those whom God designs to bring home to himself he will take care of, that they want not for the necessary expenses of their journey. When he brought them out of Egypt, and <hi type="italic">led them through the deserts,</hi> they <hi type="italic">thirsted not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.21">v. 21</reference>), for in all their removals the water out of the rock followed them; thence <hi type="italic">he caused the waters to flow,</hi> and, since rock-water is the clearest and finest, God <hi type="italic">clave the rock, and the waters gushed out;</hi> for he can fetch in necessary supplies for his people in a way that they think the least likely. This refers to what he did for them when he brought them out of Egypt; when all this was literally true. But it should now be in effect done again, in their return out of Babylon, so well provided for should they and theirs be in their return. God does his work as effectually by marvellous providences as by miracles, though perhaps they are not so much taken notice of. This is applicable to those treasures of grace laid up for us in Jesus Christ, from which all good flows to us as the water did to Israel out of the rock, for that rock is Christ. <div eID="gen16605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16606" type="x-p"/> (3.) Here is a caveat put in against the wicked who go on still in their trespasses. Let not them think to have any benefit among God's people. Though in show and profession they herd themselves among them, let them not expect to come in sharers; no (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.22">v. 22</reference>), though God's thoughts concerning the body of that people were thoughts of peace, yet to those among them that were <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> and hated to be reformed <hi type="italic">there is no peace,</hi> no peace with God or their own consciences, no real good, whatever is pretended to. What have those to do with peace who are enemies to God? Their false prophets cried Peace to those to whom it did not belong; but God tells them that there shall be no peace, nor any think like it, to the wicked. The quarrel sinners have commenced with God, if not taken up in time by repentance, will be an everlasting quarrel.  <chapter eID="Isa.48"/> <div eID="gen16606" type="x-p"/>

entries.1216411aeeeadfaf89c480f5ae7ef439cee5b6cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9241"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 48</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.48.1-Isa.48.22">Is 48:1-22</reference>. The Things That Befall Babylon Jehovah Predicted Long before, lest Israel Should Attribute Them, in Its "Obstinate" Perversity, to Strange Gods (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.1-Isa.48.5">Is 48:1-5</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen15783" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9241"/><hi type="bold">1. the waters of Judah--</hi>spring from the fountain of Judah (<reference osisRef="Num.24.7">Nu 24:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.28">De 33:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.26">Psa 68:26</reference>; Margin). Judah has the "fountain" attributed to it, because it survived the ten tribes, and from it Messiah was to spring.<div eID="gen15783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swear by ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Is 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">45:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.16">65:16</reference>).<div eID="gen15784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15785" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mention--</hi>in prayers and praises.<div eID="gen15785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not in truth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">Jr 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.24">Joh 4:24</reference>). <div eID="gen15786" type="x-p"/>
entries.dce311a7d661c791e28251d872a6f09af0740b60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9242"/><div sID="gen15787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9242"/><hi type="bold">2. For--</hi>Ye deserve these reproofs; "for" ye call yourselves citizens of "the holy city" (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">Is 52:1</reference>), but not in truth (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Is 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.11.1">Ne 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Da 9:24</reference>); so the inscription on their coins of the time of the Maccabees. "Jerusalem the Holy." <div eID="gen15787" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e5c765964404d163dc56a1c9d7c8b1afb086b33: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9243"/><div sID="gen15788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9243"/><hi type="bold">3. former--</hi>things which have happened in time past to Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.9">Is 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">44:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">45:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">46:10</reference>).<div eID="gen15788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suddenly--</hi>They came to pass so unexpectedly that the prophecy could not have resulted from mere human sagacity. <div eID="gen15789" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9bc8e096a99000ec866fc070cdfe48acbd5e889: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9244"/><div sID="gen15790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9244"/><hi type="bold">4. obstinate--</hi>Hebrew, "hard" (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.27">De 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.7">Eze 3:7</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen15790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iron sinew--</hi>inflexible (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>).<div eID="gen15791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brow brass--</hi>shameless as a harlot (see <reference osisRef="Jer.6.28">Jr 6:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.7">Eze 3:7</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen15792" type="x-p"/>
entries.c780412f32e4f0ae9117808e6751069fd3fabd2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9245"/><div sID="gen15793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9245"/>5. (See on <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Is 48:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.3">Is 48:3</reference>). <div eID="gen15793" type="x-p"/>
entries.e023a4e8d9e60d4da0c3f71afe2f1337808784e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9246"/><div sID="gen15794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9246"/><hi type="bold">6. Thou, &c.--</hi>So "ye are my witnesses" (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">Is 43:10</reference>). Thou canst testify the prediction was uttered long before the fulfilment: "see all this," namely, that the event answers to the prophecy.<div eID="gen15794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declare--</hi>make the fact known as a proof that Jehovah alone is God (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Is 44:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new things--</hi>namely, the deliverance from Babylon by Cyrus, new in contradistinction from former predictions that had been fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.9">Is 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.19">43:19</reference>). Antitypically, the prophecy has in view the "new things" of the gospel treasury (<reference osisRef="Song.7.13">So 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">Mt 13:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2Co 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Re 21:5</reference>). From this point forward, the prophecies as to Messiah's first and second advents and the restoration of Israel, have a new circumstantial distinctness, such as did not characterize the previous ones, even of Isaiah. Babylon, in this view, answers to the mystical Babylon of Revelation.<div eID="gen15796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15797" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hidden--</hi>which could not have been guessed by political sagacity (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.22">Da 2:22</reference>, 29; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen15797" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ed07372a4bd322cef0c03cc0419a09ece74dd51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9247"/><div sID="gen15798" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9247"/>7. Not like natural results from existing causes, the events when they took place were like acts of creative power, such as had never before been "from the beginning."<div eID="gen15798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even before the day when--</hi>rather [Maurer], "And before the day (of their occurrence) thou hast not heard of them"; that is, by any human acuteness; they are only heard of by the present inspired announcement. <div eID="gen15799" type="x-p"/>
entries.555193c8253044089cc45f15eb9a992baf14e800: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9248"/><div sID="gen15800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9248"/><hi type="bold">8. heardest not--</hi>repeated, as also "knewest not," from <reference osisRef="Isa.48.7">Is 48:7</reference>.<div eID="gen15800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from that time--</hi>Omit "that." "Yea, from the first thine ear did not open itself," namely, to obey them [Rosenmuller]. "To open the ear" denotes obedient attention (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.5">Is 50:5</reference>); or, "was not opened" to receive them; that is, they were not declared by Me to thee previously, since, if thou hadst been informed of them, such is thy perversity, thou couldst not have been kept in check [Maurer]. In the former view, the sense of the words following is, "For I knew that, if I had not foretold the destruction of Babylon so plainly that there could be no perverting of it, thou wouldst have perversely ascribed it to idols, or something else than to Me" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">Is 48:5</reference>). Thus they would have relapsed into idolatry, to cure them of which the Babylonian captivity was sent: so they had done (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.4">Ex 32:4</reference>). After the return, and ever since, they have utterly forsaken idols.<div eID="gen15801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15802" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wast called--</hi>as thine appropriate appellation (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen15802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the womb--</hi>from the beginning of Israel's national existence (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.2">Is 44:2</reference>). <div eID="gen15803" type="x-p"/>
entries.a60f7335bc76c03be7c82ff326b14dae3795699b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9249"/><div sID="gen15804" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9249"/><hi type="bold">9. refrain--</hi>literally, "muzzle"; His wrath, after the return, was to be restrained a while, and then, because of their sins, let loose again (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>).<div eID="gen15804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thee--</hi>that is, mine anger towards thee. <div eID="gen15805" type="x-p"/>
entries.6bad3b8aa74aec27fdf1d0ddb5e0b59bfa8ce8a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9250"/><div sID="gen15806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9250"/>10. (See on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Is 1:25</reference>).<div eID="gen15806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with silver--</hi>rather, "for silver." I sought by affliction to purify thee, but thou wast not as silver obtained by melting, but as dross [Gesenius]. Thy repentance is not complete: thou art not yet as refined silver. Rosenmuller explains, "not as silver," not with the intense heat needed to melt silver (it being harder to melt than gold), that is, not with the most extreme severity. The former view is better (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Is 1:25</reference>; 42:25; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.18-Ezek.20.22">Eze 22:18-20, 22</reference>).<div eID="gen15807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen--</hi>or else [Lowth], tried ... proved: according to Gesenius, literally, "to rub with the touchstone," or to cut in pieces so as to examine (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>; Mal 3:3; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen15808" type="x-p"/>
entries.0586e7d0c891112b320e3550250403057537ceb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9251"/><div sID="gen15809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9251"/><hi type="bold">11. how should my name--</hi>Maurer, instead of "My name" from <reference osisRef="Isa.48.9">Is 48:9</reference>, supplies "My glory" from the next clause; and translates, "How (shamefully) My glory has been profaned!" In English Version the sense is, "I will refrain (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.9">Is 48:9</reference>, that is, not utterly destroy thee), for why should I permit My name to be polluted, which it would be, if the Lord utterly destroyed His elect people" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.9">Eze 20:9</reference>)?<div eID="gen15809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not give my glory unto another--</hi>If God forsook His people for ever, the heathen would attribute their triumph over Israel to their idols; so God's glory would be given to another. <div eID="gen15810" type="x-p"/>
entries.7031cc50f972b8dad2bbd36fed2d8e388bd299b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9252"/><div sID="gen15811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9252"/>12-15. The Almighty, who has founded heaven and earth, can, and will, restore His people.<div eID="gen15811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first ... last--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Is 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">44:6</reference>). <div eID="gen15812" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0e09e3b58f3728f2a9798ccad89e3848611af9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9256"/><div sID="gen15820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9256"/><hi type="bold">16. not ... in secret--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>). Jehovah foretold Cyrus' advent, not with the studied ambiguity of heathen oracles, but plainly.<div eID="gen15820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the time, &c.--</hi>From the moment that the purpose began to be accomplished in the raising up of Cyrus I was present.<div eID="gen15821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent me--</hi>The prophet here speaks, claiming attention to his announcement as to Cyrus, on the ground of his mission from God and His Spirit. But he speaks not in his own person so much as in that of Messiah, to whom alone in the fullest sense the words apply (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.36">Joh 10:36</reference>). Plainly, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">Is 49:1</reference>, which is the continuation of the forty-eighth chapter, from <reference osisRef="Isa.48.16">Is 48:16</reference>, where the change of speaker from God (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Is 48:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.12-Isa.48.15">12-15</reference>) begins, is the language of Messiah. <reference osisRef="Luke.4.1">Lu 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.18">14, 18</reference>, shows that the Spirit combined with the Father in sending the Son: therefore "His Spirit" is nominative to "sent," not accusative, following it. <div eID="gen15822" type="x-p"/>
entries.8902d9d220bb8250c26b2b0647252862ec51e58b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9257"/><div sID="gen15823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9257"/><hi type="bold">17. teacheth ... to profit--</hi>by affliction, such as the Babylonish captivity, and the present long-continued dispersion of Israel (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">He 12:10</reference>). <div eID="gen15823" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef78b1358380ce348cf4343a2c0a1434c909c70d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9258"/><div sID="gen15824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9258"/><hi type="bold">18. peace--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.119.165">Psa 119:165</reference>). Compare the desire expressed by the same Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.42">Lu 19:42</reference>).<div eID="gen15824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">river--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Is 33:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.18">41:18</reference>), a river flowing from God's throne is the symbol of free, abundant, and ever flowing blessings from Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>).<div eID="gen15825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>religious prosperity; the parent of "peace" or national prosperity; therefore "peace" corresponds to "righteousness" in the parallelism (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Is 32:17</reference>). <div eID="gen15826" type="x-p"/>
entries.b86018f6399f2d7360f310c43fab49553c95876f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9259"/><div sID="gen15827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9259"/><hi type="bold">19. sand--</hi>retaining the metaphor of "the sea" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">Is 48:18</reference>).<div eID="gen15827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like the gravel thereof--</hi>rather, as the Hebrew, "like that (the offspring) of its (the sea's) bowels"; referring to the countless living creatures, fishes, &c., of the sea, rather than the gravel [Maurer]. Jerome, Chaldee, and Syriac support English Version.<div eID="gen15828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his name ... cut off--</hi>transition from the second person, "thy," to the third "his." Israel's name was cut off "as a nation" during the Babylonish captivity; also it is so now, to which the prophecy especially looks (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">Ro 11:20</reference>). <div eID="gen15829" type="x-p"/>
entries.77301ecd5a4f2df5a11dfc92fa7aa8c48dc69b87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9260"/><div sID="gen15830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9260"/><hi type="bold">20. Go ... forth ... end of the earth--</hi>Primarily, a prophecy of their joyful deliverance from Babylon, and a direction that they should leave it when God opened the way. But the publication of it "to the ends of the earth" shows it has a more world-wide scope antitypically; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Re 18:4</reference> shows that the mystical Babylon is ultimately meant.<div eID="gen15830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed ... Jacob--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Is 43:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">44:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen15831" type="x-p"/>
entries.baef41899c71d3b324bd4558a01ba391246234c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9261"/><div sID="gen15832" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9261"/>21. Ezra, in describing the return, makes no mention of God cleaving the rock for them in the desert [Kimchi]. The circumstances, therefore, of the deliverance from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Ex 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.20.11">Nu 20:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.15">Psa 78:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.41">105:41</reference>) and of that from Babylon, are blended together; the language, while more immediately referring to the latter deliverance, yet, as being blended with circumstances of the former not strictly applicable to the latter, cannot wholly refer to either, but to the mystic deliverance of man under Messiah, and literally to the final restoration of Israel. <div eID="gen15832" type="x-p"/>
entries.9de1d0b9baec6d793ad63257895c719b4ba56f99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9262"/><div sID="gen15833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9262"/>22. Repeated (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">Is 57:21</reference>). All the blessings just mentioned (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.21">Is 48:21</reference>) belong only to the godly, not to the wicked. Israel shall first cast away its wicked unbelief before it shall inherit national prosperity (Zec 12:10-14; 13:1, 9; 14:3, 14, 20, 21). The sentiment holds good also as to all wicked men (Job 15:20-25, 31-34). <chapter eID="Isa.48"/>

entries.a13dc0d8334fa7d3854d8362066d5b0a5588804c: <div eID="gen28428" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28429" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28430" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28430" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28429" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28431" type="x-p"/> The Jews reproved for their obstinate attachment to idols, notwithstanding their experience of the Divine providence over them; and of the Divine prescience that revealed by the prophets the most remarkable events which concerned them, that they should not have the least pretext for ascribing any portion of their success to their idols, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.1-Isa.48.8">Isa 48:1-8</reference>. The Almighty, after bringing them to the furnace for their perverseness, asserts his glorious sovereignty, and repeats his gracious promises of deliverance and consolation, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.9-Isa.48.11">Isa 48:9-11</reference>. Prophecy concerning that individual (Cyrus) who shall be an instrument in the hand of God of executing his will on Babylon, and his power on the Chaldeans; and the idols of the people are again challenged to give a like proof of their foreknowledge, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.12-Isa.48.16">Isa 48:12-16</reference>. Tender and passionate exclamation of Jehovah respecting the hardened condition of the Jewish nation, to which the very pathetic exclamation of the Divine Savior when he wept over Jerusalem may be considered a striking parallel, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.17-Isa.48.19">Isa 48:17-19</reference>. Notwithstanding the repeated provocations of the house of Israel, Jehovah will again be merciful to them. They are commanded to escape from Babylon; and God's gracious favor towards them is beautifully represented by images borrowed from the exodus from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Isa 48:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.21">Isa 48:21</reference>. Certain perdition of the finally impenitent, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.22">Isa 48:22</reference>. It will be proper here to remark that many passages in this chapter, and indeed the general strain of these prophecies, have a plain aspect to a restoration of the Church in the latter days upon a scale much greater than the world has yet witnessed, when the very violent fall of Babylon the Great, mentioned in the Revelation, of which the Chaldean capital was an expressive type, shall introduce by a most tremendous political convulsion, (<reference osisRef="Rev.16.17-Rev.16.21">Rev 16:17-21</reference>), that glorious epoch of the Gospel, which forms so conspicuous a part of the prophecies of the Old Testament, and has been a subject of the prayers of all saints in all ages. <div eID="gen28431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28432" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28433" type="x-p"/> Are come forth out of the waters of Judah "Ye that flow from the fountain of Judah" - ממי mimmey, "from the waters." Perhaps ממעי mimmeey, "from the bowels," So many others have conjectured, or מני יהודה meni yehudah, or מיהודה meyhudah, "from Judah." - Secker. But see Michaelis in Praelect, not. 22. And we have עין יעקב eyn yaakob, "the fountain of Jacob," <reference osisRef="Deu.33.28">Deu 33:28</reference>, and ממקור ישראל mimmekor yishrael, "from the fountain of Israel," <reference osisRef="Psa.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference>. Twenty-seven MSS. of Kennicott's, six of De Rossi's and two of my own, with six editions, have מימי meymey, "from the days;" which makes no good sense.
entries.a7cda536d3b5f85f34e3c0138c287616b7fc708e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28434" type="x-p"/> Thou hast heard, see all this "Thou didst hear it beforehand; behold, the whole is accomplished" - For חזה chazeh, see, a MS. has הזה hazzeh, this; thou hast heard the whole of this: the Syriac has וחזית vechazith, "thou hast heard, and thou hast seen, the whole." Perhaps it should be הנה hinneh, behold. In order to express the full sense, I have rendered it somewhat paraphrastically.
entries.fec07a5175e015c30c8c25cb166ecf70ecd3d608: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28435" type="x-p"/> And for my praise "And for the sake of my praise" - I read ולמען תהלתי ulemaan tehillathi. The word למען lemaan, though not absolutely necessary here, for it may be understood as supplied from the preceding member, yet seems to have been removed from hence to <reference osisRef="Isa.48.11">Isa 48:11</reference>; where it is redundant, and where it is not repeated in the Septuagint, Syriac, and a MS. I have therefore omitted it in the latter place, and added it here.
entries.d7719d9337803e69c0b3723c30d004a32d346aac: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28436" type="x-p"/> I have chosen thee "I have tried thee" - For בחרתיך becharticha, "I have chosen thee," a MS. has בחנתיך bechanticha, "I have tried thee." And so perhaps read the Syriac and Chaldee interpreters; they retain the same word בחרתך bechartach; but in those languages it signifies, I have tried thee. ככסף kecheseph, quasi argentum, "as silver." Vulgate. <div eID="gen28436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28437" type="x-p"/> I cannot think בכסף becheseph, With silver, is the true reading. ככסף kecheseph, Like silver, as the Vulgate evidently read it, I suppose to have been the original reading, though no MS. yet found supports this word; the similarity of the two letters, ב beth and כ caph, might have easily led to the mistake in the first instance; and it has been but too faithfully copied ever since. כור cur, which we translate furnace, should be rendered crucible, the vessel in which the silver is melted. The meaning of the verse seems to be this: I have purified you, but not as silver is purified; for when it is purified, no dross of any kind is left behind. Had I done this with you, I should have consumed you altogether; but I have put you in the crucible of affliction, in captivity, that you may acknowledge your sins, and turn unto me.
entries.3dfbb3eadafb5500d278969f6c3b40f2d6d99af5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28438" type="x-p"/> For how should my name be polluted "For how would my name be blasphemed" - The word שמי shemi, my name, is dropped out of the text; it is supplied by a MS. which has שמי shemi; and by the Septuagint, ὁτι το εμον ονομα βεβηλουται. The Syriac and Vulgate get over the difficulty, by making the verb in the first person; that I may not be blasphemed.
entries.64e32be29508948003fbe936da8551429c6d86cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28439" type="x-p"/> O Jacob "O Jacob, my servant" - After יעקב yaakob, a MS. of Kennicott's, two of De Rossi's, and the two old editions of 1486 and 1488, add the word עבדי abdi, "my servant," which is lost out of the present text; and there is a rasure in its place in another ancient MS. The Jerusalem Talmud has the same word. <div eID="gen28439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28440" type="x-p"/> I also am the last "I am the last" - For אף אני aph ani, "even I," two ancient MSS. and the ancient Versions, read ואני veani, "and I;" more properly.
entries.6865bbfda2eefc0edf4a9fd65c2ba2109262c612: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28441" type="x-p"/> Which among them hath declared these things "Who among you hath predicted these things" - For בהם bahem, "among them," twenty-one MSS., nine ancient, and two editions, one of them that of the year 1488, fourteen of De Rossi's, and one ancient of my own, have בכם bachem, "among you;" and so the Syriac. <div eID="gen28441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28442" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath loved him: he will do his pleasure on Babylon "He, whom Jehovah hath loved, will execute his will on Babylon" - That is, Cyrus; so Symmachus has well rendered it: Ὁν ὁ Κυριος ηγαπησε ποιησει το θελημα αυτου, "He whom the Lord hath loved will perform his will." <div eID="gen28442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28443" type="x-p"/> On the Chaldeans - The preposition is lost; it is supplied in the edition of 1486, which has בכשדים bechasdim, and so the Chaldee and Vulgate.
entries.1dee9e322eb91918e0b3732baaf9b27a67f3efb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28444" type="x-p"/> Come ye near unto me - After the word קרבו kirbu, "draw near," a MS. adds גוים goyim, "O ye nations;" which, as this and the two preceding verses are plainly addressed to the idolatrous nations, reproaching their gods as unable to predict future events, is probably genuine. <div eID="gen28444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28445" type="x-p"/> Hear ye this "And hear ye this" - A MS. adds the conjunction, ושמעו vashimu; and so the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate. <div eID="gen28445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28446" type="x-p"/> I have not spoken in secret - The Alexandrine copy of the Septuagint adds here, ουδε εν τοπῳ γης σκοτεινω, "nor in a dark place of the earth," as in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Isa 45:19</reference>. That it stands rightly, or at least stood very early, in this place of the Version of the Septuagint, is highly probable, because it is acknowledged by the Arabic Version, and by the Coptic MS. St. Germain de Prez, Paris, translated likewise from the Septuagint. But whether it should be inserted, as of right belonging to the Hebrew text, may be doubted; for a transcriber of the Greek Version might easily add it by memory from the parallel place; and it is not necessary to the sense. <div eID="gen28446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28447" type="x-p"/> From the time that it was "Before the time when it began to exist" - An ancient MS. has היותם heyotham, "they began to exist;" and so another had it at first. From the time that the expedition of Cyrus was planned, there was God managing the whole by the economy of his providence. <div eID="gen28447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28448" type="x-p"/> There am I "I had decreed it" - I take שם sham for a verb, not an adverb. <div eID="gen28448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28449" type="x-p"/> And now the Lord God, and his Spirit, hath sent me "And now the Lord Jehovah hath sent me, and his Spirit" - Τις εστιν ὁ εν τῳ Ησαιῳ λεγων, Και νυν Κυριος απεστειλε με και το Πνευμα αυτου; εν ᾡ, αμφιβολου οντος του ῥητου, ποτερον ὁ Πατηρ και το Ἁγιον Πνευμα απεστειλαν του Ιησουν, η ὁ Πατηρ απεστειλε τον τε Χριστον και το Ἁγιον Πνευμα το δευτερον εστιν αληθες. "Who is it that saith in Isaiah, And now the Lord hath sent me and his Spirit? in which, as the expression is ambiguous, is it the Father and the Holy Spirit who have sent Jesus; or the Father, who hath sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit. The latter is the true interpretation." - Origen cont. Cels. lib. 1. <div eID="gen28449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28450" type="x-p"/> I have kept to the order of the words of the original, on purpose that the ambiguity, which Origen remarks in the Version of the Septuagint, and which is the same in the Hebrew might still remain; and the sense whlch he gives to it, be offered to the reader's judgment, which is wholly excluded in our translation.
entries.50072f87b1474cc798763a450e5798192bb2b813: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen28450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28451" type="x-p"/> As a river "Like the river" - That is, the Euphrates.
entries.ee4fce5861dd17c598515168c15d0df43cdcc22f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen28451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28452" type="x-p"/> Like the gravel thereof "Like that of the bowels thereof" - בצאצאי מעי הים והם הדגים betseetsaey meey haiyam vehem haddagim; "As the issue of the bowels of the sea; that is, fishes." - Salom. ben Melec. And so likewise Aben Ezra, Jarchi Kimchi, etc. <div eID="gen28452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28453" type="x-p"/> His name "Thy name" - For שמו shemo, "his name," the Septuagint had in the copy from which they translated שמך shimcha, "thy name."
entries.38acc3d0b1a96caf0e0011b67dfd4a742393778b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen28453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28454" type="x-p"/> Tell this "Make it heard" - Twenty-seven MSS. of Kennicott's, (ten ancient), many of De Rossi's, and two ancient, of my own, with the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee, and Arabic, and one edition, prefix to the verb the conjunction ו vau, והשמיעו vehashmiu.
entries.d53008f59b6c35718279a4654a0337fd9926a25d: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28455" type="x-p"/> They thirsted not - through the deserts - Kimchi has a surprising observation upon this place: "If the prophecy," says he, "relates to the return from the Babylonish captivity, as it seems to do, it is to be wondered how it comes to pass, that in the Book of Ezra, in which he gives an account of their return, no mention is made that such miracles were wrought for them; as, for instance, that God clave the rock for them in the desert." It is really much to be wondered, that one of the most learned and judicious of the Jewish expositors of the Old Testament, having advanced so far in a large Comment on Isaiah, should appear to be totally ignorant of the prophet's manner of writing; of the parabolic style, which prevails in the writings of all the prophets, and more particularly in the prophecy of Isaiah, which abounds throughout in parabolical images from the beginning ts the end; from "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth," to "the worm and the fire" in the last verse. And how came he to keep his wonderment to himself so long? Why did he not expect that the historian should have related how, as they passed through the desert, cedars, pines, and olive-trees shot up at once on the side of the way to shade them; and that instead of briers and brambles the acacia and the myrtle sprung up under their feet, according to God's promises, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Isa 41:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.13">Isa 55:13</reference>? These and a multitude of the like parabolical or poetical images, were never intended to be understood literally. All that the prophet designed in this place, and which he has executed in the most elegant manner, was an amplification and illustration of the gracious care and protection of God vouchsafed to his people in their return from Babylon, by an allusion to the miraculous exodus from Egypt. See De S. Poesi, Hebr. Prael. ix.
entries.f1b4a43071ee12349b41c5b60af6915a04a3ef16: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen28455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28456" type="x-p"/> There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked - See below, note on <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">Isa 57:21</reference> (note). As the destruction of Babylon was determined, God commands his people to hasten out of it; for, saith the Lord, there is no peace (prosperity) to the wicked; ουκ εστι χαιρειν τοις ασεβεσιν, λεγει Κυριος. - Sept. "There is no rejoicing or prosperity to the wicked saith the Lord." Their is not pese to unrytous men seith the Lord. - Old MS. Bible.  <chapter eID="Isa.48"/> <div eID="gen28456" type="x-p"/>
